items.title: Beyond the Physical Card: The Software Architecture Behind MAPLE Nano
items.description: How Digital Identity, Secure Databases, Authentication, and Access Control Transform a Physical Card into a Connected Creator Identity.
items.content:
1. Introduction

A physical identity card can display information and provide a way to access a digital record. However, the real intelligence behind MAPLE Nano exists in its software architecture.

The proposed MAPLE Nano system connects a physical card to an individual’s digital MAPLE record through a secure online platform.

The card provides the entry point. The software identifies the requested record, verifies access permissions, and delivers the information that the user is authorized to see.

This article explores the proposed software infrastructure that could make this possible.

2. The Digital Identity Architecture

The foundation of MAPLE Nano is a digital identity system that connects each physical card to a corresponding digital record.

Each record could contain:

  • A unique card identifier.

  • Creator profile information.

  • OpenRockets membership information.

  • Research and project records.

  • Achievement and contribution history.

  • Access permissions.

  • Account authentication information.

The system should maintain a clear separation between publicly visible information and private account information.

For example, scanning a card could display a public creator profile, while editing personal information or accessing protected records would require authentication.

3. URL Routing and Card Verification

When someone scans the QR code, their smartphone opens a verification URL.

A possible URL structure is:

https://openrockets.com/go/OR-MN-2026-7843

The proposed process works as follows:

  1. The smartphone reads the QR code.

  2. The browser opens the MAPLE verification page.

  3. The server receives the public card identifier.

  4. The application checks its card registry.

  5. The system determines whether the card is active.

  6. The appropriate public profile or verification result is displayed.

The URL is only an entry point. The server must perform the actual verification.

A copied QR code should never be sufficient to gain access to protected account functions.

4. Backend Architecture

The backend is responsible for processing requests and coordinating communication between the physical card and the digital identity platform.

A proposed backend can contain several logical components.

A. API Layer

The API acts as the communication interface between the frontend and backend.

It receives requests, validates input, and returns appropriate responses.

Possible API functions include:

  • Card verification.

  • Profile retrieval.

  • Account authentication.

  • Card activation.

  • Card status updates.

  • Card revocation.

B. Authentication Service

This component verifies whether a person has permission to access an account.

It can support passkeys and other approved authentication methods.

C. Identity Management Service

This component manages the relationship between a card identifier and its corresponding MAPLE record.

D. Authorization Service

Authentication establishes who the user is. Authorization determines what that user is allowed to do.

For example, a visitor may view a public profile, while the account owner may edit their own information.

5. Database Architecture

The database stores and organizes the digital records associated with MAPLE Nano.

A relational database such as PostgreSQL or MySQL could support the proposed system.

Sensitive authentication secrets should not be stored as ordinary readable database values.

The database should also use appropriate access controls, backups, and protected connections.

6. Encryption and Communication Security

The communication between a smartphone and the MAPLE platform should use HTTPS with modern TLS.

TLS helps protect information while it travels between the user’s device and the server.

The proposed platform should also consider:

  • Encryption of sensitive stored information.

  • Secure password handling where passwords are supported.

  • Protected passkey registration.

  • Restricted database access.

  • Secure session management.

  • Regular security updates.

Encryption protects information, but it does not replace authentication, authorization, or responsible database management.

7. Passkey-Based Authentication

Passkeys can provide passwordless authentication for MAPLE account holders.

The user’s device protects the private cryptographic key, while the service stores the corresponding public key.

When the user signs in, the service verifies a cryptographic response to a challenge.

This means the physical MAPLE Nano card does not need to contain the user’s private authentication key.

The card identifies the relevant record; the passkey helps establish the user’s authority to access the account.

8. Access Control and Privacy

Not every person scanning a MAPLE Nano card should receive the same access.

A proposed permission model could include:

Public visitor

  • View approved public profile information.

  • View publicly shared projects and achievements.

Authenticated creator

  • Manage their own profile.

  • Update permitted information.

  • Access their private account area.

Authorized administrator

  • Manage card status.

  • Review authorized verification records.

  • Perform approved administrative operations.

Administrative access should be limited, monitored, and protected by stronger authentication.

9. Card Activation, Replacement and Revocation

A reliable identity platform must account for lost cards, replacement cards, and unauthorized use.

The proposed lifecycle could include:

  1. Card registration.

  2. Secure activation.

  3. Association with a MAPLE record.

  4. Active verification.

  5. Suspension when necessary.

  6. Revocation or replacement.

If a card is lost, an authorized account owner or administrator should be able to deactivate its identifier.

The corresponding public verification page should then report that the card is inactive or revoked.

This prevents an old physical card from remaining a trusted access credential indefinitely.

10. The Complete MAPLE Nano Software Flow

The proposed architecture can be summarized as:

SCAN → IDENTIFY → VERIFY → AUTHENTICATE → AUTHORIZE → ACCESS

  • SCAN: A smartphone reads the card’s QR code.

  • IDENTIFY: The system receives the public card identifier.

  • VERIFY: The backend checks the card registry.

  • AUTHENTICATE: The user proves their identity when required.

  • AUTHORIZE: The system checks the user’s permissions.

  • ACCESS: The platform provides the permitted information or operation.

Each stage has a distinct responsibility. Separating them makes the system easier to maintain, test, and secure.

11. Scalability and Future Development

The software architecture should be designed to support future growth.

As more creators join OpenRockets, the platform could expand through:

  • Scalable application hosting.

  • Database indexing and optimization.

  • API versioning.

  • Monitoring and audit systems.

  • Automated backups.

  • Multi-device authentication.

  • Additional verification services.

The architecture should also support future integration with other OpenRockets services, provided those integrations follow appropriate privacy and security controls.

12. Conclusion

MAPLE Nano is not simply a physical identification card. Its proposed digital architecture connects physical identification with a structured creator identity platform.

The QR code provides an entry point. The backend verifies the card. The database maintains the associated record. Passkeys support secure authentication, while authorization determines what each user can access.

The most important principle is the separation of physical identification, digital authentication, and access control.

The physical card connects the creator to their identity. The software protects that identity and manages its digital existence.

items.title: MAPLE Nano: The Architecture of Data Encoding and Digital Credentials
items.description: How QR Codes, Barcodes, Activation Keys, and Passkeys Connect Physical Identity with Secure Digital Authentication.
items.content:
1. Introduction

A physical identity card becomes useful when its printed information can connect it to a reliable digital record.

MAPLE Nano is designed to provide three important functions:

  • Identify an individual card.

  • Direct a smartphone or compatible scanner to the correct MAPLE verification record.

  • Allow the legitimate cardholder to activate and manage their digital identity securely.

The proposed architecture combines machine-readable codes with a separate digital authentication system.

2. QR Code: Two-Dimensional Data Encoding

A Quick Response (QR) code is a two-dimensional barcode that stores information in a matrix of black and white modules.

Unlike conventional barcodes, which generally encode information in one dimension, QR codes encode data in both horizontal and vertical directions.

How it works

  1. A QR generator converts the selected information into encoded data.

  2. Error-correction information is added.

  3. The data is arranged into a two-dimensional pattern.

  4. The code is printed on the physical card.

  5. A smartphone camera captures the pattern.

  6. Software identifies and decodes the information.

  7. The smartphone opens the associated MAPLE verification destination.

Proposed MAPLE Nano implementation

The QR code should contain a verification URL associated with a unique public card identifier.

For example:

https://openrockets.com/go/OR-MN-2026-7843

This is an illustrative URL, not a deployed MAPLE endpoint.

The QR code should not contain private account information, passwords, or secret activation credentials.

3. Conventional Barcode: An Alternative Identification Method

A conventional barcode provides another way to identify the card.

It represents information through a sequence of printed bars and spaces.

A compatible optical scanner measures the reflected light from the printed pattern and converts it into digital information.

Its role in MAPLE Nano

The barcode can encode the same public card identifier used by the QR verification system.

For example:

OR-MN-2026-7843

This provides an alternative identification route when QR scanning is unavailable or unreliable.

The barcode and QR code should lead to the same verification record.

4. Unique Card Identifier

Every manufactured MAPLE Nano card should have its own unique identifier.

This identifier connects the physical card to one MAPLE record.

An example format could be:

OR-MN-2026-0007843

The identifier serves as a reference key within the digital system.

It should be:

  • Unique across the card registry.

  • Non-guessable where practical.

  • Validated by the OpenRockets server.

  • Associated with one specific MAPLE record.

  • Revocable if the card is lost or compromised.

Important: A public card identifier identifies a record; it does not prove that the person presenting it owns that record.

5. Activation Keys: Separating Identification from Authority

An activation key is a separate credential used during the initial account-linking process.

The public card identifier and activation key must have different purposes.

An activation key should be generated uniquely, delivered through an appropriate protected process, and protected against reuse.

It should not be printed as readable text or placed inside a publicly accessible QR code.

6. Passkeys: Modern Digital Authentication

A passkey is a modern authentication credential based on public-key cryptography.

It uses a mathematically related pair of cryptographic keys:

  • Public key: Stored by the online service.

  • Private key: Protected by the user’s authenticator or device.

When a user signs in, the service sends a challenge. The user’s authenticator uses the private key to produce a cryptographic response. The server checks that response using the corresponding public key.

This allows authentication without transmitting a conventional password.

How passkeys could support MAPLE Nano

  1. The creator opens their MAPLE account.

  2. They register a passkey using a supported device.

  3. The service stores the corresponding public key.

  4. During future authentication, the device proves possession of the private key.

  5. The server verifies the response.

  6. Access is granted according to the account’s permissions.

A passkey is not a code that should be printed on the physical card. It is a separate digital authentication credential.

7. Encryption, Hashing and Encoding: Three Different Technologies

These concepts are often confused, but they perform different functions.

For example, converting a card ID into a QR code does not encrypt the card ID. Anyone with a suitable scanner may be able to read it.

Therefore, the security of MAPLE Nano must come from the digital authentication and verification architecture, not from the visual complexity of its printed codes.

8. The Complete Credential Architecture

The proposed architecture separates physical identification from account authority.

Physical card

  • QR code

  • Conventional barcode

  • Public card identifier

Digital verification

  • MAPLE verification URL

  • Card registry

  • Unique record association

  • Server-side validation

Account security

  • First-time activation

  • Account authentication

  • Passkey support

  • Access permissions

  • Card revocation

This separation means that copying a QR code or barcode should not automatically grant someone control over a creator’s account or intellectual property.

9. Security Considerations

The system should include:

  • Unique card identifiers.

  • Protected activation credentials.

  • HTTPS for secure communication.

  • Server-side validation.

  • Rate limits against repeated unauthorized attempts.

  • Account-level authentication for sensitive actions.

  • Audit records for activation and revocation.

  • A process to deactivate lost or compromised cards.

Public verification information should remain separate from private creator information.

10. Conclusion

MAPLE Nano combines optical data encoding with a separate digital credential architecture.

QR codes provide convenient camera-based access. Conventional barcodes provide an alternative scanning method. Unique identifiers connect the physical card to the correct digital record. Activation keys and passkeys provide separate layers of account security.

The fundamental principle is that identification must not be confused with authentication.

A card can identify a creator’s record, but only the authorized digital system should determine who can access or modify protected information.

items.title: MAPLE Nano: The Physics and Engineering Behind a Digital Identity Card
items.content:
1. Introduction

MAPLE Nano is designed to provide young creators with a physical identity credential connected to their OpenRockets MAPLE record.

The card is more than a printed identification object. Its dimensions, material composition, surface structure, printed information, and machine-readable elements must work together to provide durability, accessibility, and reliable identification.

Thanks for reading OpenRockets MAPLE Open-Source Software License for Minors! Subscribe for free to receive new posts and support my work.

This article examines the physical engineering behind the proposed MAPLE Nano card, without magnetic-stripe technology.

2. Physical Dimensions and Standards

The proposed card follows the ISO/IEC 7810 ID-1 format, commonly used for bank cards.

These dimensions make the card compatible with familiar card holders and wallets.

3. Material Science

The card can be manufactured using durable plastic materials such as PVC, PET, or polycarbonate.

  • PVC: Commonly used for conventional identification cards.

  • PET: Offers useful mechanical and environmental properties.

  • Polycarbonate: Suitable for durable, multilayer identification-card construction.

The final material should be selected according to cost, durability, printing quality, and manufacturing requirements.

4. Physical Construction and Layers

A proposed multilayer construction could include:

  1. Protective coating: Protects the printed surface against everyday wear.

  2. Printed graphic layer: Contains OpenRockets branding and cardholder-facing information.

  3. Information layer: Contains the QR code, barcode, and visible card identifier.

  4. Structural core: Provides mechanical strength and maintains the card’s shape.

  5. Rear protective layer: Protects the reverse-side printing and surface.

These are proposed manufacturing layers, not a claim that a physical production card has already been manufactured.

5. The Physics of QR Codes and Barcodes

MAPLE Nano can use two machine-readable systems.

QR Code

A QR code stores information using a two-dimensional arrangement of dark and light modules.

Its structure includes:

  • Finder patterns for locating and orienting the code.

  • Timing patterns for determining module positions.

  • Data and error-correction information.

  • Quiet zones around the printed code.

A smartphone camera captures the image, identifies the QR structure, decodes its data, and opens the associated MAPLE verification destination.

Conventional Barcode

A conventional barcode represents information through patterns of parallel bars and spaces.

A compatible scanner measures the reflected light from these patterns and converts the resulting signal into digital information.

The QR code and barcode should both direct users to the same MAPLE verification endpoint.

6. Printing and Surface Engineering

The printed elements must remain readable after repeated everyday use.

Important manufacturing considerations include:

  • High-resolution printing.

  • Adequate contrast between the code and background.

  • Sufficient clear space around machine-readable codes.

  • Scratch-resistant surface protection.

  • Consistent alignment and dimensions.

  • Testing under different lighting conditions.

A decorative design must never interfere with the scanning area.

7. What the Card Physically Contains

The proposed physical card can display:

  • OpenRockets branding.

  • MAPLE Nano identification.

  • A unique public card identifier.

  • A QR code.

  • A conventional barcode.

  • A verification website address.

Sensitive activation credentials and private account information should not be printed openly.

8. Conclusion

The physical engineering of MAPLE Nano combines material science, mechanical design, printing technology, optical scanning, and information encoding.

Its purpose is straightforward: provide a durable physical entry point to a creator’s digital identity while keeping sensitive information and intellectual-property controls within OpenRockets’ digital services.

The card identifies the destination. The digital system verifies the authority.

items.title: What happens after you scan a MAPLE Nano Card?
items.description: At a Hack Club meeting in Spain, John shows up with an idea for a small program. An orange card gives him a way to share it once it works.. Let’s find out!
items.content:
In our first Nano Diaries comic, John brings a scrap of paper to his Hack Club meeting in Córdoba, Spain. He has written three things a volunteer needs to know about a water pickup point. Where is it? How much water is ready? When did someone last check? He wants to see whether those three lines could become a program.

That is what we are designing at OpenRockets. MAPLE stands for Minor Authors’ Public License for Expression. The Nano Card is a physical starting point. OpenRockets Press gives us a place to build the publishing journey. The MAPLE research asks how a young creator can understand and manage the permissions on a piece of work that may still matter years later.

Thanks for reading OpenRockets MAPLE Open-Source Software License for Minors! Subscribe for free to receive new posts and support my work.

Show someone what you’re building

An organizer pulls up a chair and asks John to walk through the idea. They try it with two made up pickup points and realize an old count can look just as current as a new one. John makes a note to put the time beside each count. Before he leaves, the organizer hands him a Nano Card. He can scan it to see what a submission needs, then come back when he has a version someone else can try.

John can start by scanning the QR code with his phone. A club member using a shared computer could get to the same page by scanning the barcode with a compatible scanner. A scanner and browser need to work together for that route, so testing in real lab setups matters. A future card could explore an NFC tap. The proposed first card starts with codes you can scan.

Know what you are setting up

The page should explain where you are, how to set up or return to your account and what happens before a submission is visible to others. You should be able to answer basic questions before you continue. Who will see what I enter? How do I get back to my work from a different device? What happens if I am using a computer that another student will use after me?

An account also gives the service a place to take you after a mistake or an interruption. If you leave the page halfway through, the aim is to give you a clear way back. If a card is damaged or lost later, the recovery experience should help you return to your account and handle the old card. The privacy and account details are still being designed, including how the flow will respond to age and consent requirements.

Give your software a name and a home

OpenRockets Press already gives young creators a place to submit original work. The proposed MAPLE connection brings John from his card into that publishing flow. Once his tool runs, he can upload it with sample pickup points and a short guide another club can follow. He gives it a name and explains how to change a count and check when it was last updated. If someone helped write it, make sure the credit and permissions reflect their contribution.

A participating publication could appear as a submission option. A student magazine or journal could keep the way it already accepts work and add Press as another route. When you choose a publication, the submission would go through its review process. The editor might ask you for a clearer title or a simple demo. That conversation is part of turning a file into something another person can use.

Read the permissions and check the preview

If you want others to use or adapt the program, the permissions should be clear enough to read before you share it. A preview should show the title, author credit, visibility, version and the permissions attached to that version. It is an opportunity to spot a missing name, a sample file with an unwanted detail or a permission you did not mean to choose.

The public archive currently lists MAPLE 0.2.0 as a working draft. It is available to read as the research develops. It grants no permissions for a submission today. When the article refers to picking a license for a real program, it means an applicable license available for use and permissions you have the right to grant.

Give readers a link they can come back to

When a participating publication accepts the work, the published page would give the file somewhere to be found and cited. A reader should be able to see which version they are reading, who made it and what the stated permissions are. If you later publish an improved version, the two versions should be identifiable on their own. The original permissions remain part of the original publication record. A later version gives you a fresh place to describe what changed.

A good record should be just as useful to you. You might change schools and lose access to a device. You might want to show someone the work you made at fifteen, long after you made it. You should have a way to find the record again and understand what a reader sees. That is the continuity MAPLE is designed to explore.

Try it with something small

Start with a tiny tool you understand well. Write one sentence about what it does. Ask a friend what they would need in order to run it and how they would know which version they found. The answers will tell you a lot about what useful publishing looks like.

If you brought a project to your next Hack Club meeting, what would you ask someone to try first? Their answer could become the first line of the instructions you publish with it.

items.title: Nano Diaries #1: John and the card that kept his work
items.description: A young creator from a club table to a published program that helps neighbors get drinking water.
items.content:
The card on the folding table

John went to the club because he wanted to show someone a scrap of paper. He had written three lines at the top. The first said where something was needed. The second said how much. The third said when someone had last checked. He didn’t have a name for the program yet. Most of it still lived on that scrap.

A Hack Club organizer looked at the three lines and slid an orange card across the table. She wore a tiny orange cap. There was a spare beside her, so John put it on. The organizer told him the card was a place to begin. He could scan it when he was ready and see how a piece of software could be shared.

Thanks for reading OpenRockets MAPLE Open-Source Software License for Minors! Subscribe for free to receive new posts and support my work.

John tried the square code with a phone camera. The next day he showed a friend a second route. A barcode on the card could take a student with a compatible scanner and shared computer to the same starting page. In the first design, the codes do the work. A tap with NFC could be explored for a later card.

On the first page John could read what the card opened, what setting up an account would involve, and what would happen before any work could be made public. He made his way through the account setup and verification steps. He had an account he could return to when he was ready to submit.

What the paper became

John showed his friend Mina the scrap. She asked him why the third line was there. He said that a number without a time could be wrong before anyone noticed. If a person had checked a pickup point at noon, someone arriving at dusk needed to know that. Mina said the time should be on the screen in plain sight.

The school sometimes helped at a neighborhood water collection point after storms. A volunteer would call another volunteer to ask which sites had full jugs. John built a small browser tool where a coordinator could update each pickup point, the number of jugs ready, and the time of the last check. On paper it still looked like three lines. On a screen it gave people one list they could read without making a round of calls.

Before the work goes public

John opened the submission flow through OpenRockets Press. He uploaded the program and a short note explaining what it did. A student journal was available in the imagined pilot, so he chose it. The journal would decide whether to publish the submission. On the preview he checked the title, the version number and the credit for Mina’s contribution. He also checked that the example contained made up locations and numbers.

John wanted other clubs to be able to use and improve the code. He read the permissions before choosing a license that was available for use. MAPLE 0.2.0 is currently a working draft. While its terms are being developed, a real submission would use an applicable license the creator can grant. In John’s story, the preview gave him a moment to read the terms and see exactly what a reader would be able to find.

The editor tried the demo. She asked John to put a clear example of the time format in his instructions. John fixed it and sent it back. When the journal accepted the work, its page gave the program a link, a title, a version and a clear place to read the license. John wrote the link on the back of the scrap.

The evening it mattered

When a storm left part of a nearby town without running water, a coordinator at a distribution point found John’s program through the journal. She adapted a copy for her team and entered the pickup points they had already arranged. A volunteer was headed to a hall with empty shelves. The coordinator could see that another hall had just received more water. She called the volunteer, who turned the cart around and took the full jugs to the families who were waiting.

The people at the hall did the work. John’s three lines helped them decide where to go while there was still time to make the trip. When he heard about it, what stayed with him was that it happened in a town he’d never visited. The coordinator could find the program, see how to use it and build on it because the work had a place to live.

The next orange cap

John eventually dropped his card in a puddle. By then he knew the card had opened the way to his account. With a recovery route, he could return to his record and arrange to disable or replace the damaged card. He could still find the work and the published page. In the years that followed he improved the tool. The original version remained identifiable, including the permission it had been published with, while readers could see where the newer version began.

At another club event, a younger student came up to the same kind of folding table. She showed John a small sheet of paper with three marks on it. He asked what the marks meant. She told him. John reached for a fresh card and the spare orange cap.

The next student’s work could be something completely different. She could still start at the same table.

items.title: OpenRockets MAPLE nano: A Card. Worth Keeping, and Gifting...
items.description: The MAPLE Nano Card gives young creators a simple place to start. OpenRockets is building a way for their work to stay connected to them as they grow.
items.content:
Picture a student who writes their first useful program at a school club. A few years later, someone finds it and wants to build on it. What if they could see who made it, find the version they used and understand how they may share it? That is the future we are working toward with MAPLE, the Minor Authors’ Public License for Expression.

Thanks for reading OpenRockets MAPLE Open-Source Software License for Minors! Subscribe for free to receive new posts and support my work.

A first step that fits in your hand

We have begun introducing the Nano Card to young creators through Nano Diaries. The next design starts with two ways in. A student with a phone can use a QR code. A student with access to a compatible school scanner can use a barcode. Both routes are designed to open the same web experience. We’re also exploring NFC for a future card. The two scannable routes are where we’re starting.

We want this first step to feel just as natural at a club meeting as it does at a technology event. A student can pick up the card, see where it leads and learn what happens before they share their work.

A home for the work

OpenRockets Press already gives young creators a place to submit original work. We’re designing the connection from the Nano Card to that publishing experience, starting with software. Imagine a student sending a program to a participating student journal and, if it is accepted, getting a page they can point to later. The page could bring together the author credit, the published version and the permissions attached to it. A reader would know what to cite and where to begin if they wanted to build on it.

We want that record to be useful to the person who made the work, too. They should be able to come back to it when they switch devices, when they change schools and when they are ready to show what they made years earlier.

Permissions that are easier to understand

We’re developing MAPLE as a software licensing framework with young creators in mind. The public 0.2.0 working draft invites readers to follow the research as we work toward a license that makes permissions easier to understand. Starting with software gives us concrete examples to work through, from a student’s first program to a project with several contributors.

What would you want a reader to know about something you made at fifteen? Who helped build it? How should they credit you? What can they do with the code? Those are the questions we want a young creator to feel comfortable asking from their first submission onward.

Follow Nano Diaries and the MAPLE draft as they develop. If you know a student who is building something they’re proud of, share this with them. We’d love to hear what would make it easier for them to share their work and find it again.

Explore Nano Diaries

Protecting what people create is just as important to us as helping them create it. This is personal. One of our team members remembers making origami as a child, only to lose the photographs that recorded those creations years later. It is a small story, but it speaks to something larger. The work young people make can be meaningful, original, and worth preserving, even when there is no lasting place to keep it.

That belief helped shape OpenRockets Press. We want young creators to have reliable ways to publish their code, research, art, and other original work while keeping their ownership and recognition. Above all, we want their creations to remain accessible to them as they grow into adulthood.

We also build technology that makes the internet more useful and welcoming for young people. Interkid Browser and Interkid.org focus on a safer browsing experience, while projects such as Scienteen explore new ways to share research and creative ideas. Across all of these efforts, our purpose remains the same: to help good ideas endure and give the people behind them room to do more.

Our Mission

We believe young people can create work of real value when they are trusted, encouraged, and given the right tools. We want OpenRockets to become a dependable part of the infrastructure behind organizations doing good, especially those whose ambitions are much bigger than their resources.

Our work brings together software, science, education, publishing, and nonprofit support. Through it all, we are guided by two commitments: helping nonprofits achieve more, and helping young creators protect and retain access to their intellectual property.

items.title: MAPLE NANO: Turning a Physical Card into a Digital Identity
items.description: How OpenRockets can connect physical membership, NFC technology, software engineering and digital identity through a single intelligent card.
items.content:
1. Introduction

The MAPLE NANO Card is a concept proposed by Nesapriyan to provide every young creator with a durable physical credential connected to their OpenRockets MAPLE record.

MAPLE, which stands for Minor Authors’ Public License for Expression, focuses on protecting and documenting intellectual property created by minors.

The card is designed to act as a convenient gateway to a creator’s verified profile and registered work. Rather than storing sensitive information directly on the card, it connects users to OpenRockets’ digital services, where the authoritative records, authentication and access controls are maintained.

2. Three Ways to Access a MAPLE Record

To support different devices and scanning capabilities, MAPLE NANO is designed around three access methods:

QR Code – Camera Access

Allows compatible smartphones to scan the card and open the corresponding MAPLE verification page.

Barcode – Alternative Access

Provides another way to identify the card using compatible barcode scanners or applications.

        user="root",

    email = data["email"]
    password = data["password"]

items.title: To Reduce Poverty, We Must Lower The Friction Of Invention. Minors Are The Best Inventors In The World
items.description: There are about 1.3bn children have no internet connection in their lives. This is happening in the age of supercomputing and AGI. The best way to solve this problem is to make inventing frictionless
items.content:
From coding and engineering to app development and art, the creative potential of youth knows no bounds. However, legal age barriers often complicate the contracts needed to protect and govern their innovations. What could be achieved if legal frameworks evolved to match the speed of a young creator's imagination?

That is why we set out to approach this challenge from the ground up.

Thanks for reading OpenRockets MAPLE Open-Source Software License for Minors! Subscribe for free to receive new posts and support my work.

Introducing OpenRockets MAPLE, a nonprofit initiative developed by the OpenRockets MAPLE team, Arjun J and Neksha. Conceived as a pioneering semi-open-source licensing framework for minors, MAPLE aims to help young innovators protect their intellectual property and create freely, with clearer ways to protect, manage and distribute their work.

MAPLE seeks to make intellectual property guidance and licensing protection accessible across all ages, locations and family incomes because meaningful access to these rights should not depend on a creator’s circumstances.

Greater confidence could free young people to experiment productively, share ideas and contribute to future technologies, research and the prosperity of their communities and countries. The opportunity is not limited to financial returns. Its deeper value lies in helping more young ideas reach the world.

The Fundamental Problem: Young Creators and Intellectual Property

The challenge begins when minors who create original software, engineering mechanisms, applications, artwork or technology encounter the complex legal apparatus of intellectual property. Many must navigate it without the experience or resources available to adult creators.

Imagine a ten-year-old whose open-source software attracts a major corporation. The company may want to integrate it into products, modify it, redistribute it or build upon it. What happens next depends on two things: the permissions granted and the young developer’s ability to manage them.

Copyright law generally protects the original expression in software, including its source code. However, copyright does not automatically protect the underlying ideas, technical methods, or inventions, which may require other forms of intellectual property protection, such as patents.

The difficulty increases when the creator tries to govern use through legally binding agreements. In most places, contracts involving minors are may be void, voidable or subject to additional requirements, creating uncertainty about licensing, negotiations, compensation and enforcement.

A large corporation may possess the financial resources, legal expertise, and institutional support necessary to navigate these complexities. A thirteen-year-old developer often does not.

The imbalance is not necessarily in the value of the work. It is in the resources available to negotiate and defend the rights surrounding it.

Established open-source licenses, including the MIT License and Apache License 2.0, provide valuable rules for using and distributing software. MAPLE draws on ideas from these frameworks while focusing specifically on the legal circumstances of minors.

One notable exception in terms of guidance is Creative Commons, which explicitly discusses whether children can apply its licenses.

Many licenses do not specifically address the circumstances of minors. This highlights an important uncertainty: owning copyright and having confidence in the legal arrangements governing its use are not always the same thing.

For a young creator, that uncertainty can create an uncomfortable question:

“What if distributing and protecting my work becomes difficult, and I cannot do anything about it?”

That concern should not become a barrier to innovation.

MAPLE Is More Than a License: It Is About Freedom

MAPLE aims to do more than supply licensing terms. At its center is freedom.

Freedom is one of the four core structural pillars upon which MAPLE is being built.

Freedom to experiment, collaborate, and innovate without becoming overwhelmed by complicated legal procedures.

And, most importantly, freedom to focus on creating something extraordinary.

A student developing a drone-navigation algorithm should be able to focus on accuracy, efficiency and real-world applications instead of spending countless hours fearing unauthorized commercialization. MAPLE seeks to reduce that distraction.

MAPLE aims to reduce the cognitive friction of innovation: the stress and mental effort created by unclear ownership, unfamiliar contracts, licensing terms, infringement concerns and expensive disputes. Clearer guidance about rights and sharing could return attention to the creative process.

If young creators spend less time navigating uncertainty, more of their energy can go into experiments, collaborations, and ambitious projects. Over time, that could expand the range of ideas brought into the wider innovation ecosystem.

After all, OpenRockets believes innovation should be driven by curiosity, not by the complexity of the legal mechanisms surrounding it.

The Essential Value of MAPLE

Original work does not suddenly become worth protecting when its author turns eighteen. MAPLE’s essential value is to help minors create, improve and distribute their work with less legal friction and a clearer understanding of their rights and permissions. Young people’s software, research, art and engineering can contribute to society just as adults’ work does. Without practical guidance, promising ideas may stay private or be shared on terms their creators do not understand.

The goal is not to commercialize every young invention. It is to give creators meaningful choices about sharing, reuse and protection, so more of their ideas can reach communities, collaborators and future research.

Copyright Ownership

Across most of the world, original creative works automatically receive copyright protection the moment they are created, without requiring formal registration.

A thirteen-year-old can own an original computer program, musical composition, artwork or novel; age alone does not erase authorship or ownership.

Copyright ownership identifies the legal rights holder, but it does not resolve every challenge of licensing, commercializing or enforcing those rights.

Legal Capacity

The next question is not who owns the work, but which agreements that owner can legally enter.

Although minors can legally own intellectual property, their ability to enter into binding contracts may be limited by the laws of their respective countries.

Established frameworks like the MIT License, Apache License 2.0, and Creative Commons (CC BY-NC 4.0) are designed to govern general distribution and reuse, but none of them are built around the legal capacity of minors. MAPLE addresses this gap directly by placing minor-specific IP protection at the center and pinnacle of open-source licensing.

The Difference Between Void and Voidable Contracts

Countries approach contracts involving minors differently.

Some jurisdictions may treat an agreement as void from the start, while others may allow a minor to disaffirm a voidable agreement. Because contractual capacity varies by jurisdiction, protective licensing approaches must account for local law.

Void and voidable contracts have different consequences. An invalid or disaffirmed license does not remove the creator’s copyright or grant unlimited permission for others to use.

Even so, representation, licensing disputes and enforcement can remain difficult and create friction. A minor may own exceptional IP yet struggle to negotiate commercial use, secure compensation or pursue remedies without adult assistance.

This gap between ownership and practical control is where MAPLE seeks to contribute.

The Missing Layer in Existing Licensing Frameworks

The gap is not a total absence of copyright, but a shortage of accessible licensing support designed around minors. General-purpose frameworks grant useful permissions yet rarely guide young creators through parental authorization, contractual capacity, commercial licensing, ownership disputes or affordable enforcement.

Imagine a fifteen-year-old who builds a sophisticated scientific simulation tool and receives an offer from a commercial research platform. The developer may need a copyright license, contributor agreement, confidentiality agreement or revenue-sharing contract. Appropriate terms could preserve ownership, define permitted uses, reserve separate commercial permissions and establish royalties or other compensation. A parent, guardian or legal representative may need to participate, depending on local law.

How many teenagers understand these instruments, and how many families can afford an IP attorney? That imbalance between valuable work and practical control is where MAPLE seeks to help.

MAPLE aims to make licensing more accessible through clearer terms and practical protective guidance, potentially including guardian authorization, ownership records, commercial-use permissions and dispute-resolution support. The aim is not to bypass national rules or turn every student into a legal expert, but to help young creators understand their rights, share responsibly and exercise greater control.

What Makes MAPLE Different?

Most open-source licenses concentrate on the permissions granted to people using a work. They generally say little about minors’ distinct circumstances: contractual capacity, the role of guardians, control over distribution, and practical enforcement. Children can already own copyright and use existing licenses; the gap is in making those rights understandable and usable without leaving young creators to navigate legal complexity alone.

MAPLE explicitly aims to serve young creators across ages, regions and financial circumstances. Its proposed distinction is a licensing approach designed around their needs, seeking clearer choices about lawful distribution and support for exercising rights. By reducing that friction, MAPLE could create more room for minors to innovate alongside experienced creators. It does not promise that a single license can override national laws or automatically secure enforcement.

A Real-World Example: Young Developers and Bargaining Power

This is not merely theoretical. Reporting has documented allegations of excessive workloads and inadequate contractual safeguards for young contributors. An investigation by The Guardian examined these concerns among Roblox developers, who can create, distribute and monetize games on the platform.

One developer, Anna, contributed to a project generating substantial revenue after beginning to make games at a young age. According to the investigation, changes to payment arrangements amid limited formal contractual protection caused a significant reduction in her compensation.

Another developer, Regan Green, described pressure to work extensively and alleged the threat of replacement if he did not meet expectations; the project leader disputed the allegation about threats. The investigation also raised concerns about limited safeguards and dispute-resolution options.

These accounts raise concerns about work and compensation. They also show how a young person can devote years to a valuable project without comparable bargaining power, legal knowledge or institutional support. Better legal clarity and guidance could reduce that vulnerability.

Why Access to IP Protection Matters

A creator’s ability to defend intellectual property can depend on circumstances unrelated to the quality of the idea. Three inequalities are especially important.

Financial Inequality

For minors from financially disadvantaged backgrounds, an existing legal right may be difficult to exercise. Some families have money, technical knowledge and access to IP lawyers for contracts, negotiation or legal action. Others lack the resources or familiarity with the legal system needed to challenge a larger organization.

Imagine two students who independently build equally creative applications. One family can hire legal professionals; the other struggles to afford basic advice. The students may hold similar copyright rights, yet differ sharply in their practical ability to defend them.

OpenRockets believes innovation should not depend on the financial resources of a child’s family.

MAPLE aims to reduce this disparity by making intellectual property guidance and licensing mechanisms more accessible.

Regional Differences

Legal rules, procedures, resources and enforcement vary across countries, so the experience of protecting IP can differ considerably by region.

A student with accessible legal aid, established IP institutions and educational resources may find protection easier than an equally capable student facing expensive representation or weak awareness. The divide can exist between countries and between urban and rural communities, creating unequal opportunities.

An innovator in an under-resourced community deserves meaningful protection just as one in a prestigious laboratory does. MAPLE’s ambition is a framework adaptable across jurisdictions, without pretending their laws are identical.

Limited Knowledge of the Legal System

Many children and parents do not fully understand the differences between copyright ownership, licensing permissions, patents, commercial agreements and legal enforcement.

Publishing source code online does not automatically authorize unrestricted use. A young creator may nonetheless choose a license that permits commercial reuse when the intention was to reserve those rights, or accept unfavorable contractual terms without understanding the consequences.

Such gaps in legal knowledge add cognitive friction and divert attention from building, experimenting and developing ideas. MAPLE seeks to make rights and licensing more understandable, accessible and practical for everyone.

A Regional Example: Innovation in the UAE

Students around the world participate in STEM, robotics, software development, engineering and entrepreneurship. Countries such as the United Arab Emirates encourage innovation in drones, artificial intelligence and other STEM fields.

A growing innovation ecosystem also needs clear, practical pathways for minors to understand and exercise their rights.

Imagine a fourteen-year-old in the UAE creating an autonomous drone-navigation system with original software, engineering diagrams and technical components. Different elements may warrant different protections: code and original drawings may qualify for copyright, while genuinely patentable inventions can require separate patent protection.

The UAE has established intellectual property laws. Federal laws in the UAE address categories of original work, including software and applications.

OpenRockets aims to bridge existing legal protections and the open-source licensing world through practical guidance and mechanisms that make rights easier to understand and exercise.

Understandable legal guidance can matter as much as the opportunity to build.

The goal is to help more young people understand and benefit from existing protections, regardless of location, family finances or familiarity with legal terminology.

MAPLE’s Vision: Freedom to Create, Capacity to Protect

OpenRockets MAPLE aims to change how minors experience intellectual property protection, helping them develop, share and manage their work with confidence. Its central ambition remains FREEDOM.

Freedom to create.

Freedom to experiment.

Freedom to publish ambitious projects without unnecessary anxiety.

And freedom to understand, manage, and defend their intellectual property with greater confidence.

By reducing cognitive friction and making legal protection clearer, MAPLE seeks to narrow the gap between owning intellectual property and being able to manage it.

OpenRockets’ ambition extends beyond a single license: young creators everywhere should have access to meaningful intellectual property guidance and protection.

Future Ambitions

OpenRockets is designing MAPLE for a future in which minors can protect and, where legally possible, enforce rights in their own intellectual work, improve their creations and decide how to distribute them. With clearer permissions and less uncertainty, a young innovator could spend more time refining a product, collaborating or pursuing research. Ideas that might otherwise remain unseen could find new paths into technology, science and communities.

The longer-term ambition extends beyond protection for minors alone. OpenRockets hopes to help develop a more seamless innovation ecosystem in which young people and adults can create, share and build on intellectual work together. Removing avoidable barriers between generations could encourage new forms of collaboration and accelerate research and development. That is a future-oriented objective, not a claim that legal systems already offer identical protection or that innovation must produce a financial return.

Whether a student writes software in the UK, experiments with robotics in the United Arab Emirates, creates digital artwork in India or builds a scientific instrument elsewhere, age should not prevent understanding and exercising rights. OpenRockets aims to pursue this vision across countries, income levels, educational settings and communities.

No single license can eliminate every legal obstacle or guarantee enforcement. Meaningful progress will require collaboration with legal professionals, educators, policymakers and the wider open-source community. Even so, a framework designed for young creators could be a step toward a more equitable innovation ecosystem.

OpenRockets’ mission is to ensure that minors need not choose between sharing their creativity and protecting their work. It seeks to reduce legal barriers, expand IP knowledge and help young people develop ambitious ideas into meaningful creations.

Innovation does not have an age requirement.

The freedom to create should not have one either.

Another developer, Regan Green, described pressure to work extensively and alleged the threat of replacement if he did not meet expectations; the project leader disputed the allegation about threats. The investigation also raised concerns about limited safeguards and dispute-resolution options.

These accounts raise concerns about work and compensation. They also show how a young person can devote years to a valuable project without comparable bargaining power, legal knowledge or institutional support. Better legal clarity and guidance could reduce that vulnerability.

Why Access to IP Protection Matters

A creator’s ability to defend intellectual property can depend on circumstances unrelated to the quality of the idea. Three inequalities are especially important.

Financial Inequality

For minors from financially disadvantaged backgrounds, an existing legal right may be difficult to exercise. Some families have money, technical knowledge and access to IP lawyers for contracts, negotiation or legal action. Others lack the resources or familiarity with the legal system needed to challenge a larger organization.

Imagine two students who independently build equally creative applications. One family can hire legal professionals; the other struggles to afford basic advice. The students may hold similar copyright rights, yet differ sharply in their practical ability to defend them.

OpenRockets believes innovation should not depend on the financial resources of a child’s family.

MAPLE aims to reduce this disparity by making intellectual property guidance and licensing mechanisms more accessible.

Regional Differences

Legal rules, procedures, resources and enforcement vary across countries, so the experience of protecting IP can differ considerably by region.

A student with accessible legal aid, established IP institutions and educational resources may find protection easier than an equally capable student facing expensive representation or weak awareness. The divide can exist between countries and between urban and rural communities, creating unequal opportunities.

An innovator in an under-resourced community deserves meaningful protection just as one in a prestigious laboratory does. MAPLE’s ambition is a framework adaptable across jurisdictions, without pretending their laws are identical.

Limited Knowledge of the Legal System

Many children and parents do not fully understand the differences between copyright ownership, licensing permissions, patents, commercial agreements and legal enforcement.

Publishing source code online does not automatically authorize unrestricted use. A young creator may nonetheless choose a license that permits commercial reuse when the intention was to reserve those rights, or accept unfavorable contractual terms without understanding the consequences.

Such gaps in legal knowledge add cognitive friction and divert attention from building, experimenting and developing ideas. MAPLE seeks to make rights and licensing more understandable, accessible and practical for everyone.

A Regional Example: Innovation in the UAE

Students around the world participate in STEM, robotics, software development, engineering and entrepreneurship. Countries such as the United Arab Emirates encourage innovation in drones, artificial intelligence and other STEM fields.

A growing innovation ecosystem also needs clear, practical pathways for minors to understand and exercise their rights.

Imagine a fourteen-year-old in the UAE creating an autonomous drone-navigation system with original software, engineering diagrams and technical components. Different elements may warrant different protections: code and original drawings may qualify for copyright, while genuinely patentable inventions can require separate patent protection.

The UAE has established intellectual property laws. Federal laws in the UAE address categories of original work, including software and applications.

OpenRockets aims to bridge existing legal protections and the open-source licensing world through practical guidance and mechanisms that make rights easier to understand and exercise.

Understandable legal guidance can matter as much as the opportunity to build.

The goal is to help more young people understand and benefit from existing protections, regardless of location, family finances or familiarity with legal terminology.

MAPLE’s Vision: Freedom to Create, Capacity to Protect

OpenRockets MAPLE aims to change how minors experience intellectual property protection, helping them develop, share and manage their work with confidence. Its central ambition remains FREEDOM.

Freedom to create.

Freedom to experiment.

Freedom to publish ambitious projects without unnecessary anxiety.

And freedom to understand, manage, and defend their intellectual property with greater confidence.

By reducing cognitive friction and making legal protection clearer, MAPLE seeks to narrow the gap between owning intellectual property and being able to manage it.

OpenRockets’ ambition extends beyond a single license: young creators everywhere should have access to meaningful intellectual property guidance and protection.

Future Ambitions

OpenRockets is designing MAPLE for a future in which minors can protect and, where legally possible, enforce rights in their own intellectual work, improve their creations and decide how to distribute them. With clearer permissions and less uncertainty, a young innovator could spend more time refining a product, collaborating or pursuing research. Ideas that might otherwise remain unseen could find new paths into technology, science and communities.

The longer-term ambition extends beyond protection for minors alone. OpenRockets hopes to help develop a more seamless innovation ecosystem in which young people and adults can create, share and build on intellectual work together. Removing avoidable barriers between generations could encourage new forms of collaboration and accelerate research and development. That is a future-oriented objective, not a claim that legal systems already offer identical protection or that innovation must produce a financial return.

Whether a student writes software in the UK, experiments with robotics in the United Arab Emirates, creates digital artwork in India or builds a scientific instrument elsewhere, age should not prevent understanding and exercising rights. OpenRockets aims to pursue this vision across countries, income levels, educational settings and communities.

No single license can eliminate every legal obstacle or guarantee enforcement. Meaningful progress will require collaboration with legal professionals, educators, policymakers and the wider open-source community. Even so, a framework designed for young creators could be a step toward a more equitable innovation ecosystem.

OpenRockets’ mission is to ensure that minors need not choose between sharing their creativity and protecting their work. It seeks to reduce legal barriers, expand IP knowledge and help young people develop ambitious ideas into meaningful creations.

Innovation does not have an age requirement.

The freedom to create should not have one either.

items.title: Arjun Explains: What Is OpenRockets MAPLE and the Upcoming MAPLE Nano Card
items.description: What OpenRockets MAPLE Is and Why the MAPLE nano Card Matters
items.content:
OpenRockets MAPLE began with a simple problem. Young people are already writing software, conducting research, designing technology, and creating work that can have real value. Yet the systems used to document, license, preserve, and manage intellectual property were largely built around adults and organizations. For someone under 18, owning an idea or a piece of software can be very different from understanding how it can be licensed, how permission should be granted, how attribution should work, and how the work can remain connected to its creator years later. MAPLE, which stands for Minor Authors Public License for Expression, is OpenRockets attempt to build infrastructure around that gap. The goal is not merely to create another software license. The larger ambition is to make it easier for young creators to document what they have made, understand the permissions surrounding it, and preserve a clear connection between a creator and their work as that work travels through the world. OpenRockets

Thanks for reading OpenRockets MAPLE Open-Source Software License for Minors! Subscribe for free to receive new posts and support my work.

In a recent OpenRockets explanation, team researcher Arjun Jamgade described MAPLE as part of a much wider idea about authorship and intellectual history. A young person might create a research project, a simulation, an engineering design, or a piece of software today, and years later another person might discover it and build something new from it. The problem is that this chain of contribution can become difficult to reconstruct when work is poorly documented or when the creator does not have access to the same legal and technical resources as someone working inside a large institution. OpenRockets wants MAPLE to make authorship, permissions, documentation, and preservation easier to understand. The long term vision is an ecosystem where young creators can participate in science and technology without their age, financial circumstances, geography, or access to professional support automatically determining how well their work is protected or remembered.

The MAPLE nano card is intended to turn that idea into something physical and accessible. OpenRockets plans for the card to create a direct link between a child and the MAPLE system. Through camera codes and a dedicated web interface, a creator would be able to connect intellectual property with OpenRockets and indicate how they want that work managed. The current plan is for registered intellectual property to be hosted through GitHub and issued the OpenRockets MAPLE nano pre release License, while the licensing information can continue to be updated as the MAPLE system develops. The important idea is not the card itself. The card is an entry point. Instead of intellectual property management beginning with complicated documents, unfamiliar systems, or access to professional legal resources, OpenRockets is exploring whether a young creator could begin with something as simple as a physical card connected to a digital system. MAPLE is still developing, and OpenRockets describes its wider licensing work as an effort to make intellectual property protection for minors more understandable and usable. OpenRockets

The first public introduction of this direction will also connect with OpenRockets Shanghai. With special permission from Shanghai Children’s Medical Center, the event is planned for November 3, 2026, in the GW130 Presentation Room. The purpose is to bring together young inventors inside the hospital, including children who are already building remarkable things, and give them a place to meet, share, and create. During the event, OpenRockets plans to introduce the MAPLE NFC card as an early step toward a wider MAPLE ecosystem. That matters because the philosophy behind MAPLE is not that every child needs to build a famous invention. That every young creator should have a reasonable opportunity to document what they created, understand what happens to it, and decide how other people may interact with.

There is still a great deal to build. MAPLE will require technical work, collaboration, legal expertise, testing, and participation from communities in different countries. But the direction is becoming clearer. OpenRockets is trying to connect licensing, preservation, publishing, authorship, and physical access into one system designed with young creators in mind. The MAPLE nano card represents one of the first attempts to make that system tangible. OpenRockets Shanghai will be an early place to introduce it directly to young inventors. Volunteers currently living in Shanghai, Hangzhou, and surrounding areas are also being welcomed to help support the event. More information will be released through OpenRockets Open Source, and people interested in volunteering can join through the OpenRockets website. The larger goal remains the same. A young person should be able to create something important and have a practical way to keep that work connected to who created it.
