items.title: Open-Source Hasn't Solved Ageing (And That’s Okay! Mistakes Happen)
items.description: Built by OpenRockets & teenagers aged 11 to 16, MAPLE is our attempt to create the world’s first open-source software license for kids, giving them high authority over their intellectual property.
items.content:
Open Source Has an Age Problem.

Every day, teenagers write software, publish research, build open-source projects, create designs, organize technical communities, and contribute work that can travel much further than the bedroom, classroom, library, refugee camp, or school computer where it was created. The technology works. The internet works. Git works. GitHub works. Open source works. Then the young creator reaches the point where the system stops being about writing code and starts becoming about legal agreements, intellectual property transactions, delegations of rights, institutions, companies, and the adults legally expected to participate around them. That is where the system changes.

We are a group of teenagers between the ages of 11 and 16 working through Scientific Teenager by OpenRockets Inc. For months, we have been working around one mission: protecting minors’ intellectual property and preventing young creators from losing access to or rights over what they create, while preserving the beauty and openness of open-source science. The project we believe can move that mission forward is OpenRockets MAPLE 1.0, the Minor Authors’ Public License for Expression. Our goal is ambitious. MAPLE is designed to become the world’s first open-source software license dedicated to minor authors and to become indexable on the Linux Foundation’s SPDX License List, the industry-standard software license list. We do not think the software world needs another license because there are not enough licenses. We think it needs MAPLE because an entire category of creators has never had a license designed around them.

The Missing Layer

Most of the infrastructure surrounding open-source software quietly assumes something about the person using it. It assumes that when legal participation becomes necessary, the correct adult exists, that adult is available, that adult understands the technology, that adult supports what the child is doing, and that the relationship between that child and that adult is healthy enough for participation to happen. For millions of young people, those assumptions can fail. When legal agreements with institutions or companies, intellectual property transactions, or delegations of rights require parental participation on behalf of a minor, the technical quality of what that young person created can suddenly become almost irrelevant.

The code can be brilliant. The project can work. The repository can exist. The young person can understand every line they wrote. But the next stage can depend on circumstances completely unrelated to the work itself. We call this friction. Friction sounds harmless until you understand who experiences it, because something that appears to be a minor procedural inconvenience can become the point where a young creator simply cannot move forward.

The Reality of Human Ambition

Sometimes the clearest way to understand this problem is to look at what young people continue to build when the assumptions around an ordinary childhood disappear. United Nations Refugee Agency documented the story of Remy Gakwaya, who fled Burundi at the age of 15 after his parents were killed in ethnic clashes. He eventually reached the Dzaleka refugee camp in Malawi, learned programming, and founded TakeNoLab to teach other refugees coding and application development. Resources were so limited that some students practiced using printed images of computer keyboards because there were not enough computers, while power cuts sometimes meant classes continued in the dark. Remy’s story matters because it demonstrates something fundamental: human ambition does not wait for ideal circumstances. A young person can lose almost every form of stability around them and still continue creating, learning, and building.

But the same underlying problem does not only appear in refugee camps or extreme circumstances. A senior software engineer who later worked across major technology and engineering companies wrote to us about his own experience as a teenager. At 15, he worked part-time after school to save for an 8080-based computer called a Compucolor II. His father, a systems engineer at IBM, matched his savings dollar for dollar, and his older brother was already a software developer. One day, after an argument over a household chore, his mother grabbed the keyboard connected to the machine. Because the keyboard was attached by a ribbon cable to the converted 19-inch monitor, the computer came crashing from the desk onto the floor and was severely damaged. He told us that he subsequently left home, moved in with a friend of his brother, and successfully pursued legal emancipation. Before that incident, by his own account, he had lived a reasonably good life with his parents.

That story is important precisely because it is not a story about an obviously broken household. A supportive father had helped him buy the computer. His brother was already in software. He had a home. He had access to technology. And yet, in a single moment, circumstances completely unrelated to the quality or legitimacy of what he was building changed his relationship with the tools and property behind his work. His eventual route was emancipation, a legal mechanism that can give some minors greater authority over themselves and their property. But emancipation is not globally available, and even where it exists, it is hardly an ordinary or realistic path for most young creators. The point is not that every young developer will experience something this dramatic. The point is that systems built around the assumption that the correct adult will always be available, supportive, and capable of acting in a young creator’s interests are making an assumption that reality cannot guarantee.

WAIT. What happens to the child who does not have reliable family support? What happens to the young programmer without a stable home? What happens to the teenager creating software inside a refugee camp? What happens to the student using a school computer because there is no computer waiting at home? What happens when the person legally expected to participate in protecting or managing a young creator’s work is also the person restricting their access to that work? We recently spoke with a student connected to Asha Trust in Kanpur, India, who is organizing a hackathon using infrastructure provided by OpenRockets. He spoke to us about what it feels like to be alone as a kid. These are not theoretical edge cases to us.

In the United States, about 1,540,000 school-aged students are homeless. Globally, about 150,000,000 minors are homeless. More than 273,000,000 minors are either abandoned or subjected to severe parental negligence. Now put those numbers beside a system that can require the participation of the right adult when a minor reaches important legal interactions involving what they created. That is why we refuse to dismiss this as a small inconvenience. The inconvenience can become the barrier.

Open-Source Did Not Solve Age. And That’s Okay! Mistakes Happen.

One of the beautiful things about open source is that geography matters less. A teenager in South Africa can publish code that someone in California uses. A student in India can collaborate with someone in Melbourne. A young developer who has never entered a corporate office can build something used by people they will never meet. Open source broke down enormous barriers to participation. But there is still an age boundary hidden underneath that openness.

The modern open-source ecosystem has spent decades developing licenses that define permissions, restrictions, attribution, redistribution, modification, patents, compatibility, and countless other questions. Those licenses are extraordinarily important. But none of that means the particular realities of minor authorship disappear. That is the missing layer we are trying to build. MAPLE is not an attempt to pull minors away from open source. MAPLE exists because we want minors to participate in open source more safely, more confidently, and with infrastructure that recognizes that the author on the other side of a repository might be thirteen years old. We believe that if minors are already building the future of software, the licensing infrastructure of software must eventually acknowledge that they exist.

Why MAPLE

MAPLE stands for the Minor Authors’ Public License for Expression. Our goal is to create an open-source license specifically designed around minor authorship. We want MAPLE 1.0 to become indexable on the Linux Foundation’s SPDX License List. We want to reach a stage where major software platforms can recognize it. We want to eventually be able to approach platforms such as GitHub and say that minor authorship should not remain an invisible edge case inside infrastructure used by millions of developers. Ultimately, we want a young person creating something important to have an option designed with people like them in mind.

There is a reason we chose licensing as the place to attack this problem. A license travels with the work. A license can be recognized by infrastructure. A license can become standardized. A license can appear inside development tools. A license can become something developers, organizations, institutions, lawyers, and platforms learn to recognize. The problem should not have to be rediscovered from zero every single time another thirteen-year-old creates something valuable. The infrastructure should already be there. That is what we are trying to build.

This Is Not a School Project

We need to make something very clear. We are not doing this for a medal. We are not entering MAPLE into a competition. We are not trying to complete another IB project. We are trying to establish something we believe should continue existing after we grow up. If MAPLE succeeds, the people who benefit most from it may be children we will never meet. That is the point.

We have no formal backing. There is no giant institution behind this campaign. There is no enormous marketing budget. There is no organization capable of simply declaring that this matters and forcing the technology industry to pay attention.

More Than 18,000 People Are Receiving What you are Reading Right Now.

Our Substack now has more than 18,000 subscribers. So we want to ask you to imagine something. Imagine if only one percent of the people receiving this decided that this problem was worth supporting. That is 180 people. For an established movement, 180 people might look small. For something at our stage, it can change the conversation. When we eventually approach people in Silicon Valley, open-source communities, standards organizations, lawyers, researchers, and platforms such as GitHub, one of the most important things we need to prove is very simple: other people believe this needs to exist too.

That is why we are asking you to do something incredibly small. If you use X, formerly Twitter, follow @MAPLElicense. If you agree with something we publish, like it. If you think another developer should see it, repost it. If you disagree with us, quote it and tell us why. Visibility matters because eventually this idea has to reach people with the ability to help turn it from a project created by teenagers into infrastructure recognized by the software world. If you do not use X, sign our petition at Change.org/LicenseU18. There are about 16 signatures right now. Your name will not disappear inside a petition containing millions of signatures. At this stage, every signature materially changes what we can show when we say that people want this problem addressed.

If You Are an Adult, Help Us Build This Right

MAPLE is being built by teenagers, but we do not believe teenagers should build something this important inside an echo chamber. If you are an adult with experience in technology, open source, software development, law, education, research, nonprofit work, product development, policy, or simply years of experience inside the technology world, we would like you to consider joining the OpenRockets MAPLE Advisory Board. You do not need a particular degree, job title, university background, or professional certification. You do not need to be a lawyer. You do not need to be an executive. If you understand open source, care about young creators, and believe your experience could help us make better decisions, that is already valuable to us.

As an advisor, your role is to guide us, question us, challenge our assumptions, share what you have learned, point out what we are missing, and help us think more carefully before we make important decisions. Talk with us. Ask difficult questions. Tell us when an idea does not make sense. Help us understand how the software industry actually works. Help us understand how developers, companies, institutions, open-source communities, and the people who maintain the infrastructure we use may respond to what we are building. We want MAPLE to remain a project led by young people, but strengthened by adults who are willing to give those young people the benefit of experience.

If you would like to become an advisor, please fill out the form at OpenRockets.com/join and mention that you are interested in joining the MAPLE Advisory Board. You can also contact us directly at opensource@openrockets.com. We will try to respond within one to three days and, where appropriate, invite you into our Discord and Slack communities so you can speak directly with the teenagers working on MAPLE.

Advisors who contribute their time and knowledge to the project will also be able to receive an official letter of gratitude and involvement from OpenRockets, recognizing their advisory service and contribution to our nonprofit community. But more importantly, you will have the opportunity to help a group of young people think more clearly, avoid mistakes, understand industries they have not yet had decades to experience, and build something that we hope will eventually outlive all of us.

What We Want to See One Day

Our goal can ultimately be reduced to one very simple image. A child somewhere opens GitHub. Maybe they are eleven. Maybe they are thirteen. Maybe they are sixteen. Maybe they are sitting inside a comfortable home with two supportive parents. Maybe they are sitting inside a rural school. Maybe the computer belongs to somebody else. Maybe they have no idea where they will be living next year. None of that changes what appears on the screen. They create a repository, open Choose a license, and there, alongside licenses recognized throughout the software world, they see: OpenRockets MAPLE 1.0 Universal.

That is the future we are trying to build, and we need enough people behind this idea to get there. If you believe minors belong in the future of open source, do not just agree with this article and close the tab. Follow @MAPLElicense. If you do not use X, sign Change.org/LicenseU18. If you know somebody in open source, intellectual property, software infrastructure, technology policy, or Silicon Valley who needs to see this, send this article to them. You can read our essay Why Is It So Easy to Ignore? at openrockets.com/research/maple/v1, and you can also read TechCity’s coverage, OpenRockets: Continuity and Protection of the Intellectual Property of Minors.

items.title: Casgevy: When CRISPR Moves Into Early Childhood
items.description: The next phase of gene editing has begun
items.content:
The next phase of gene editing has begun

For decades, sickle cell disease and transfusion-dependent β-thalassemia have been treated largely by managing their consequences rather than correcting the underlying genetic biology. That paradigm changed with Casgevy (exagamglogene autotemcel), an autologous genome-edited cell therapy based on CRISPR-Cas9.

In December 2023, Casgevy became the first FDA-approved CRISPR-based therapy. On July 1, 2026, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration expanded its indication to patients 2 years and older with sickle cell disease accompanied by recurrent vaso-occlusive crises or transfusion-dependent β-thalassemia. The decision made Casgevy the first gene therapy approved by the FDA for children as young as two with sickle cell disease. But the significance of Casgevy is not simply that CRISPR is being used in children. The deeper scientific achievement is that researchers are using genome editing to reprogram a patient’s own blood-forming stem cells so that they produce a different hemoglobin program

Understanding the biological problem

Sickle cell disease is fundamentally a disorder of hemoglobin. Hemoglobin is the oxygen-carrying protein inside red blood cells. The most important adult form, hemoglobin A, contains β-globin chains encoded by the HBB gene. In sickle cell disease, pathogenic variants in HBB produce abnormal hemoglobin, particularly hemoglobin S. When oxygen concentration falls, hemoglobin S can polymerize inside red blood cells. This changes the cells from their normal flexible shape into rigid, sickle-like cells. The consequences occur at multiple biological levels:

HBB mutation → abnormal hemoglobin → hemoglobin polymerization → red-cell deformation → vascular obstruction → tissue ischemia → vaso-occlusive crisis

Repeated episodes can contribute to progressive damage involving organs such as the kidneys, lungs, brain and spleen. β-thalassemia has a different molecular mechanism. Mutations affecting β-globin production result in insufficient β-globin synthesis, leading to ineffective erythropoiesis and severe anemia. Some patients therefore require regular red-blood-cell transfusions. Casgevy approaches both diseases through a different biological route. Instead of directly repairing the patient’s disease-causing HBB mutation, it attempts to restore a protective developmental hemoglobin program

.

The key: fetal hemoglobin

Before birth, humans primarily produce fetal hemoglobin (HbF). HbF consists of two α-globin chains and two γ-globin chains:

HbF = α₂γ₂

After birth, the body normally switches toward adult hemoglobin production:

HbA = α₂β₂

This developmental switch is controlled by a complex regulatory network. One of the most important regulators is BCL11A, a transcription factor that suppresses γ-globin expression after birth. This creates an intriguing therapeutic opportunity. If γ-globin production can be reactivated, cells can produce more HbF. And HbF has a crucial property:

It does not participate in the same sickling process as hemoglobin S. Therefore, increasing HbF can reduce the tendency of red blood cells to sickle. Casgevy exploits this biology.

What CRISPR actually edits

Casgevy is not designed to randomly modify the genome. The therapy uses CRISPR-Cas9 to target a regulatory region associated with BCL11A, specifically an erythroid-specific enhancer. This distinction matters. The treatment does not simply “delete BCL11A.” Instead, editing the regulatory enhancer reduces BCL11A activity in erythroid cells—the cells that ultimately become red blood cells. The resulting molecular chain is approximately:

CRISPR-Cas9 editing

↓

BCL11A erythroid enhancer disruption

↓

reduced BCL11A-mediated repression

↓

γ-globin expression increases

↓

HbF production increases

↓

red blood cells become more resistant to sickling

For β-thalassemia, increased HbF and total hemoglobin production can reduce or eliminate the need for regular transfusions. This is an important conceptual distinction:

Casgevy does not necessarily repair the original mutation. It changes the regulatory environment surrounding hemoglobin production.

Why the patient’s own stem cells are used

Casgevy is an autologous hematopoietic stem-cell therapy. That means the patient’s own blood-forming stem cells are collected rather than using cells from a donor. The relevant cells are CD34-positive hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells. These cells are capable of repopulating the blood-forming system. The treatment process therefore begins outside the body.

Step 1 — Mobilization

Doctors first stimulate hematopoietic stem cells to move from the bone marrow into the bloodstream.

Step 2 — Apheresis

Blood is circulated through an apheresis machine that separates the desired stem-cell population.

The collected cells are transported for manufacturing.

Step 3 — CRISPR editing

The patient’s cells are exposed to the CRISPR-Cas9 editing system.

The system recognizes the intended DNA target associated with the BCL11A erythroid enhancer.

Cas9 generates a targeted DNA break, after which the cell’s DNA-repair machinery creates the intended regulatory disruption.

Step 4 — Quality control

The manufactured cell product must meet specifications before it can be returned to the patient.

This is fundamentally different from giving someone a conventional tablet.

The “drug” is essentially a population of the patient’s own living cells that has been genetically modified outside the body.

Step 5 — Conditioning

Before the edited cells are infused, the patient’s existing bone marrow is prepared using myeloablative conditioning with busulfan.

This creates physical space in the marrow for the edited stem cells to engraft.

This step is also one of the major burdens of the treatment.

Step 6 — Reinfusion

The edited cells are administered intravenously.

Once they reach the bone marrow, successful engraftment allows them to generate new blood cells.

Step 7 — Hematopoietic regeneration

Over time, descendants of the edited stem cells produce red blood cells containing elevated HbF.

The objective is not a temporary pulse of HbF.

The objective is to establish a new, self-renewing blood-forming system from edited stem cells.

What happened in pediatric trials?

The 2026 FDA expansion was supported by pediatric clinical data. In children 5 to under 12 years old with sickle cell disease, the FDA reported 11 enrolled patients, of whom 8 were evaluable for the primary efficacy endpoint. All eight evaluable patients achieved the primary endpoint:

100% achieved at least 12 consecutive months without protocol-defined severe vaso-occlusive crises during the specified evaluation period.

The median duration without severe VOCs was 17.5 months, with individual durations ranging from 13.2 to 21.3 months among these patients. For transfusion-dependent β-thalassemia, 15 children aged 5 to under 12 were evaluated, with 9 considered efficacy-evaluable. 8 of those 9 patients achieved at least 12 consecutive months of transfusion independence, with a median duration of transfusion independence of 20.1 months. These numbers are striking, but they must be interpreted correctly. The pediatric studies are relatively small and open-label. They provide strong evidence of biological and clinical activity, but they cannot provide the same statistical certainty as a very large randomized trial.

Why approve treatment at age two?

This may be the most important scientific question. Why not wait until children are older? Because disease damage can accumulate. Sickle cell disease does not suddenly become harmful when someone reaches adulthood. Recurrent vaso-occlusion and chronic hemolysis can affect organs throughout childhood. The FDA specifically highlighted the rationale that earlier treatment may reduce the risk of lasting end-organ damage. However, there is an important regulatory nuance. The clinical efficacy data supporting the pediatric expansion were generated primarily in children aged 5 to under 12. The FDA extended the indication down to age 2 through extrapolation using the available clinical data and product characteristics rather than because a large clinical trial had independently demonstrated efficacy in thousands of two-year-olds.

That distinction is scientifically important.

The treatment is powerful—but it is not simple

Calling Casgevy a “one-time treatment” can create the impression that the procedure is as simple as receiving an injection. It is not. The treatment involves stem-cell mobilization, apheresis, manufacturing, chemotherapy conditioning, cell infusion and prolonged medical monitoring. The conditioning regimen is particularly significant. Patients receive myeloablative busulfan, which suppresses existing bone marrow so that the edited cells can establish themselves. Consequently, some of the major adverse effects associated with treatment are related to the transplantation-like process rather than CRISPR editing alone. The FDA lists mucositis and febrile neutropenia among common adverse reactions. The labeling also contains warnings concerning neutrophil engraftment failure, delayed platelet engraftment, hypersensitivity and the possibility of off-target genome editing

Teenage boy revels in ‘freedom’ after £1.65 million gene-editing treatment

The off-target editing problem

CRISPR’s greatest strength—its ability to modify DNA at a selected sequence—is also accompanied by an important scientific question: What happens at genomic locations that resemble the intended target? These are called potential off-target sites. An unintended edit could theoretically alter gene regulation or cellular behavior. This does not mean Casgevy has been shown to cause such an outcome in routine use. Rather, it represents a long-term biological uncertainty that must be monitored because the edited hematopoietic stem cells can persist and continue producing blood cells for many years. The FDA therefore includes off-target genome editing as a warning and requires long-term follow-up. This illustrates an important principle of genome medicine: The treatment may be administered once, but its biological consequences can last for decades.

Casgevy is not simply “fixing DNA”

One of the most interesting aspects of Casgevy is the therapeutic philosophy behind it. There are two broad strategies for genetic disease:

Strategy A — Correct the disease mutation

Repair the pathogenic DNA sequence itself.

Strategy B — Modify the biological system around the mutation

Change another regulatory pathway so that the disease phenotype becomes much less severe.

Casgevy largely represents Strategy B.

The sickle-cell mutation remains.

Instead, the therapy changes hemoglobin regulation so that the red blood cell contains substantially more protective fetal hemoglobin. This demonstrates something fundamental about modern genetics: Treating a genetic disease does not always require correcting the original mutation. Sometimes the more powerful intervention is to identify a regulatory pathway that can compensate for the mutation.

Why Casgevy could change medicine beyond sickle cell disease

Casgevy is important not only because of its clinical results. It demonstrates a complete therapeutic pipeline:

patient → cell collection → genome editing → manufacturing → conditioning → reinfusion → stem-cell engraftment → long-term biological effect

That pipeline could become a framework for other diseases involving blood-forming stem cells. The broader field is moving toward therapies in which cells are treated as programmable biological systems. Instead of designing only a chemical molecule, researchers can potentially design: a genetic instruction + a delivery system + a cellular population capable of carrying that instruction forward. That represents a fundamental shift in pharmacology.

The unanswered questions

Despite the extraordinary progress, several questions remain.

1. How durable is the effect?

Casgevy is intended to provide a long-lasting effect, but patients treated recently have not yet been observed for their entire lifetimes.

2. What happens after decades?

Long-term surveillance is essential because edited hematopoietic stem cells can persist for years.

3. Can the treatment become easier?

The current process requires specialized centers, cell manufacturing and intensive conditioning.

Reducing these barriers could be as important as improving the editing technology itself.

4. Can genome editing become cheaper?

A therapy involving individualized cell collection, manufacturing and transplantation is fundamentally different from manufacturing a conventional tablet at enormous scale.

5. Can editing eventually occur directly inside the body?

That is one of the major directions of the broader gene-editing field.

The larger significance

Casgevy represents more than a new treatment for two blood disorders. It demonstrates that a patient’s own stem cells can be genetically reprogrammed outside the body and returned as a living therapeutic system. The July 2026 pediatric expansion pushes that technology into an especially important stage of medicine: early childhood. For a two-year-old, the objective is not simply to treat another episode of disease. It is potentially to intervene before years of cumulative biological damage have occurred. That is the deeper promise of genome editing.

The first generation of gene therapies asked: Can we replace a defective gene?

CRISPR introduced a more powerful question: Can we precisely rewrite the biological instructions controlling a cell?

Casgevy provides one of the clearest clinical demonstrations that the answer can be yes. And as genome editing becomes more precise, more scalable and more accessible, the boundary between treating disease and redesigning cellular function may become one of the defining frontiers of 21st-century medicine.

items.title: When Minors Create, Who Owns the Innovation?
items.description: Exploring the gap between invention and ownership with OpenRockets’ MAPLE 1.0
items.content:
Every winter, the Society for Science announces a new group of Regeneron Science Talent Search (STS) finalists. These young scientists are introducing discoveries that have the potential to change the face of science–from AI screening tools to diagnose disorders like autism to testing potential cancer treatment using clam models.

We celebrate these teenagers as the future of modern medicine. They stand on stages, pose for photos, and receive praise from pioneers of their respective fields.

Thanks for reading OpenRockets MAPLE Open-Source Software License for Minors! Subscribe for free to receive new posts and support my work.

But behind the scene lies a contradiction. We trust these minors to revolutionize how we view oncology, engineering, and epidemiology, yet our legal systems dictate that they are not mature enough to take ownership of their creations. In the eyes of the world, a teenager who designs a groundbreaking medical device cannot independently sign a patent, execute a licensing agreement, or protect their discovery from potential exploitation.

Regeneron Science Talent Search 2026. Image from societyforscience.org

Today, in order to bring their ideas to life, a student researcher may not rely solely on their community’s resources. They require assays such as centrifuges and high powered microscopes, to name a few. This leads them to university laboratories, working under the supervision of a Principal Investigator (PI).

Before setting foot in the lab, a student is handed an onboarding packet filled with dense rules of legal liability and property rights.

For an adult, this is a standard protocol. For a high school student, however, signing this paper means accepting responsibilities they don’t fully understand. If we truly want to foster a generation of bright, independent innovators, the scientific communities must build something to protect our future scientists.

Closing the Gap: Introducing MAPLE

MAPLE License (Minor Authors Public License for Expression) dedicates their philosophy to this exact framework. Created by OpenRockets, a nonprofit infrastructure services provider, the license was born out of a problem the team experienced firsthand. They watched their early digital creations and projects vanish due to expired accounts, platform closures, and a lack of legal standing. OpenRockets Team recognized that minors do not have the power to own their discoveries. MAPLE introduces Legal Capacity Continuity (LCC) around the recognition that while a teenager may be a minor today, their intellectual property belongs entirely to them. This license ensures their authorship turns into full legal ownership the moment they turn 18.

If a mind is capable enough to discover a cure, they are capable enough to own it. When a student changes the course of medicine, their name will no longer be buried under the institutions that capitalized on their findings for profit. By securing the rights of the youngest minds today, we give the future back to the very hands building it.

items.title: A Child Made This. What Happens Next?
items.description: MAPLE, young creators, and the work we should help them keep.
items.content:
Neksha DeSilva remembers making origami as a child. He no longer has the creations, or the photographs that might have let him return to them.

In a profile of OpenRockets, where he serves as CTO, he described that loss: “Nobody took any of it from me. It simply was not held by anything.”

That sentence stayed with me. Work can disappear without anyone stealing it. A device gets replaced. An account is forgotten. Something a child spent weeks making becomes something they can only describe.

We encourage children to create. We are less consistent about helping them decide what happens afterward.

Software makes that question particularly interesting. A teenager’s program can travel through projects and products they will never see. The code may survive while its connection to the person who wrote it grows harder to trace.

MAPLE, the Minor Authors Public License for Expression, is OpenRockets proposed response. Its current petition describes public software permissions paired with a notice preserving the work’s origin: its author, project, original publication date, and origin in minor authorship. The intention is for that record to accompany downstream copies.

There is something worth examining here. A first project can become part of someone’s creative history long before they have a professional identity. Keeping its origins legible gives that person a better chance of finding their way back to it.

The legal starting point matters, though. In the United States, the Copyright Office says minors can claim copyright and receive registrations, while state laws may govern related business dealings. Young creators already have rights. Understanding and exercising them can require help.

Existing licenses also preserve authorship information. MIT requires copyright and permission notices to remain in copies or substantial portions of the software. Apache 2.0 has attribution requirements, including provisions for a supplied NOTICE file.

So MAPLE needs to answer a fair question: what would a new license preserve more effectively than an established license with better documentation? Public review could clarify which problems belong in licensing, and which need better tools, archives, or guidance. The answer should determine the design.

“Open source” needs equal care. The petition’s title says “semi-open-source”; its body describes an ambition to grant ordinary open-source freedoms. Under the Open Source Initiative’s definition, licenses cannot exclude business use or discriminate against people or groups. Recording a minor’s authorship and restricting who may use their software are different choices.

Then come the questions that are easy to miss in an enthusiastic announcement.

How much should a child have to disclose to receive credit? An origin notice should not casually become a demand for a birth date, school, or identity document. A creator may want their work recognized under a pseudonym.

And what happens when they grow up? Someone returning to a project at twenty-one needs to understand what choices remain available. Other developers need to understand the permissions they received. The history of a work should remain accurate while leaving room for its author to change.

These are questions for the eventual license, rather than benefits we can already assume. MAPLE is a proposal; its terms need review. SPDX recognition is a stated goal, and its inclusion principles require stable text. An ambition is one stage of the work.

Preservation brings us back to the missing origami. OpenRockets describes Press as a place to publish young creators’ work with identifiers for referencing it. But an identifier cannot keep a file alive by itself. The ARK Alliance explicitly explains that persistence requires continuing management.

Someone still has to maintain the archive, fund it, and arrange for the work to survive changes in the team. That responsibility lasts much longer than the excitement of launching a project.

This is why I think MAPLE deserves attention and careful scrutiny. It asks us to consider the life of a young person’s work beyond the moment we applaud it.

We should not require that work to become a breakthrough before we care. An awkward game or a modest program may matter deeply to the person who made it.

Years later, they may want to open the first version again.

We should help make sure it is still there.

items.title: The Future Has Arrived. But Who Gets to Create It?
items.description: In a world where ideas can change humanity, should a young person's age determine how far their ideas can go?
items.content:
Every great invention begins somewhere.

Sometimes, it begins in a research laboratory. Sometimes, in a garage. And sometimes, it begins with a young person who has an idea but doesn’t yet know how to bring it to life. But what happens when that young creator finally builds something meaningful? Who protects their work? How can they share it with the world? And should being young make it harder for them to participate in innovation? These questions bring us to an initiative by OpenRockets: MAPLE, a project focused on creating a semi-open-source software license designed to protect the intellectual property of minors.

Why Does This Matter?

We often encourage young people to think creatively, solve problems, and build things that matter. But we don’t always consider what happens after they create something. A student might develop a software application, design a new tool, or contribute an original idea to an open-source project. Their work may represent months of learning, experimentation, and effort. Yet understanding intellectual property, software licenses, and the rules governing how work can be shared is not always easy especially for someone just starting out. Young creators need opportunities to learn, collaborate, and share their work while understanding the rights and responsibilities involved.

Innovation should encourage young people to create, not leave them uncertain about what happens to their creations.

Why MAPLE Deserves Attention

OpenRockets has described MAPLE as an effort to create a semi-open-source license specifically designed to protect minors’ intellectual property. The idea raises an important question: can we make the world of software creation more accessible to young people while giving greater attention to protecting their original work? Open-source development has helped people learn from existing projects, collaborate across borders, and build new ideas together. But sharing work and protecting the interests of its creator are also important considerations. A license intended for minors could contribute to this conversation. Its practical impact will depend on the final license terms, how it interacts with existing intellectual property laws, and how effectively it can be used in different countries. It is also important to recognize that a license alone cannot resolve every legal challenge young creator may face. Awareness, appropriate guidance, and accessible educational resources matter too. Still, the question behind MAPLE is worth discussing: how do we make it easier for young people to participate in innovation without overlooking their rights?

This Is About More Than Software

Think about the young people who are learning to code today. Some are building their first websites. Others are experimenting with artificial intelligence, designing applications, or contributing to projects alongside people from different countries. They are not simply preparing to become tomorrow’s innovators. They are already learning, creating, and contributing. When we create better ways for young people to understand and protect their work, we help them approach innovation with greater awareness and confidence. That benefits more than individual creators. It can also encourage collaboration, strengthen learning communities, and help young people participate more meaningfully in the global technology ecosystem. The goal should not be to protect ideas by preventing them from being shared. It should be to help creators understand how they can share, collaborate, and protect their work responsibly.

A Question for the Future

Technology is advancing rapidly. Young people are finding new ways to build software, explore artificial intelligence, and solve problems that matter to them. But our systems for supporting young creators must evolve alongside these opportunities. If we encourage a young person to invent something, we should also help them understand what it means to own, share, and protect their creation. Because the next meaningful innovation might not come from an established company or a famous research institution. It might come from someone writing their first program in their bedroom, experimenting after school, or building something with friends. They deserve the opportunity to explore that potential—and the knowledge to navigate the responsibilities that come with creating something original.

The future does not wait for people to grow up before ideas begin to matter.
